observations.title: Handbook: Revenue recognition
observations.publisher: KPMG LLP, U.S. Department of Professional Practice
entity_roles: contractors and other vendors reporting customer contracts
accounting_bases: financial GAAP interpretation; ASC 606 and 340-40
observations.source_classification: December 2025 U.S. GAAP interpretive handbook reproducing ASC 606 excerpts and implementation examples; professional guidance, not the authoritative Codification itself or proof of the latest edition
questions: How does a job-cost measure of progress differ from allowable-cost billing and incurred-cost settlement?
How do contract assets, receivables and contract liabilities relate to performance and billing?
When can an over-time service contract be shown as WIP versus a contract asset or receivable?
When may variable consideration associated with a customer contract enter the Topic 606 transaction price, and what happens when that estimate changes?
How does a change in transaction price affect revenue already recognized for satisfied or partially satisfied performance obligations?
observations.inspected_summary: KPMG's ASC 606 Example 19 describes a $5.0 million building refurbishment contract with $4.0 million expected costs, including $1.5 million of procured elevators. Because elevator cost would overstate progress, the contractor excludes it from the cost-to-cost measure and recognizes the elevator transfer at zero margin. With $0.5 million of other cost incurred against $2.5 million remaining measured costs, progress is 20 percent: $0.7 million revenue on adjusted transaction price plus $1.5 million elevator revenue, $2.2 million total revenue, and $2.0 million cost. KPMG also explains that contract assets/liabilities are presented net per contract, unconditional rights are receivables, and recognized performance before an unconditional right produces a contract asset; amounts received or due before performance produce a contract liability. The guide says over-time performance does not create a separate WIP asset when the customer controls the asset as it is created; the entity records a contract asset or receivable as revenue is recognized. These are financial-reporting principles, separate from FAR allowable-cost and billing rules. The December 2025 guide also explains that variable consideration is included only subject to the significant-reversal constraint and that a change allocated to a satisfied or partially satisfied performance obligation is recognized as revenue or a reduction in the period of change. It explicitly says invoicing does not determine whether the right to payment is unconditional; legal rights, contract terms, and the facts and circumstances control.
